# Your first project {#your-first-project}

::: {.doc-lead}
Bring a plot into a figure. Give it a caption, a place in your manuscript, and a moment in your presentation. The same work stays connected throughout.
:::

<div class="guide-meta"><span>About 20 minutes</span><span>All five workspaces</span><span>Beginner</span></div>

You’ll need [Flux installed](/install/). The plotting step uses Python and fluxplot; you can also begin with an SVG or PNG you already have. All numbers in the small example below are **synthetic**.

Shortcuts are written with **Ctrl** and **Alt**. On macOS, press **⌘ Command** for Ctrl and **⌥ Option** for Alt; [Keyboard shortcuts](/docs/shortcuts.html) lists them all.

## 1. Give the work a home {#create}

Create a working folder called `growth-study`. In Flux, choose **New project** from Home and create a project named `paper` inside that folder.

```text
growth-study/
└── paper/         ← your Flux project
```

Your analysis code will live in `growth-study`; the project holds the writing, plots, figures, references, and slides. Flux autosaves your work. If saving reports an error, resolve it before closing the app.

You can return to the project from Home, or open it from a terminal:

```bash
flux /path/to/growth-study/paper
```

[Learn how projects and files fit together](projects-and-files.qmd).

## 2. Make a plot with named parts {#plot}

In a terminal, move to `growth-study` and create a Python environment:

```bash
uv init
uv add fluxplot
```

Save the following as `make_growth.py` beside the `paper` folder. You use ordinary matplotlib axes; fluxplot adds a stable name to each series and saves the semantic files.

```python
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import fluxplot as fp

time = [0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24]
control = [0.02, 0.05, 0.13, 0.41,
           0.95, 1.60, 1.90]
treatment = [0.02, 0.07, 0.25, 0.80,
             1.50, 1.95, 2.10]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 3.2))
fp.line(ax, time, control,
        series="control",
        marker="o", label="Control")
fp.line(ax, time, treatment,
        series="treatment",
        marker="s", label="Treatment")
ax.set(xlabel="Time (h)",
       ylabel="Illustrative response")
ax.set_title("Synthetic growth profiles")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()

here = Path(__file__).resolve()
plots = here.parent / "paper" / "plots"
plots.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
recipe = {"script": str(here),
          "params": {}, "inputs": []}
fp.save(fig, plots / "growth.svg",
        recipe=recipe)
```

Run it:

```bash
uv run python make_growth.py
```

You now have three neighboring files in `paper/plots/`: `growth.svg`, `growth.fluxplot.json`, and `growth.recipe.json`. Keep them together. The SVG is the visible plot; the manifest describes its parts and data; the recipe records its producing script.

::: {.doc-note}
**Already have a plot?** Import any SVG or PNG to continue. Per-part editing and data morphs require semantic information, which fluxplot records when it creates a plot.
:::

## 3. Compose and refine in Figure {#figure}

Switch to **Figure** in the titlebar. Open the **Plot gallery** with **Alt+G**, select `growth.svg`, and choose **Insert**. Flux imports at the plot’s physical size; the gallery marks semantic plots with a **◆** badge.

Select a plot part with **Ctrl+click**. Press **F** to open its properties and change a line’s stroke color. **Alt+R** opens **X-ray**, where you can inspect the plot’s named parts and regeneration recipe.

Try changing a number in `make_growth.py` and rerunning it. Flux refreshes the linked plot, retaining styling attached to stable series identities such as `control`. Source status in the figure catalog tells you whether the link is current, missing, or needs attention.

Open **Figure-Meta** with **Alt+M** and add a caption. For this example: “Synthetic growth profiles for two illustrative conditions. Points show constructed values at seven time points; lines connect successive observations.”

## 4. Collect and read a reference {#read}

Open **Library** and paste a paper’s DOI into the add field, or import a BibTeX file. The reference joins your shared library, where it is available across projects. Use **Enrich** for additional metadata and the download control for an available open-access PDF.

Open the paper in **Reader** from its Library row. Select a sentence and choose a highlight color, then attach a note to the highlight. Reader also supports tabs, side-by-side reading, and figure snips that retain their source provenance.

A reference in your Library becomes part of a project’s bibliography when you cite it. [Library and project references](projects-and-files.qmd#library) explains the distinction.

## 5. Write with the figure in view {#write}

Switch to **Paper** and write a short paragraph. Three insertions connect the document to your work:

- Type **`/figure`** and choose your figure to embed it with its caption.
- Type **`@@`** to insert a cross-reference to the figure in your prose.
- Type **`@`** and an author’s name to choose a citation from your library.

Figure numbering follows the designation you choose in Figure. Reordering paragraphs does not renumber your figures. The permanent reference stays attached when you rename a figure or move it between canvases.

Your manuscript remains a `.qmd` file. You can write equations, add tables, keep working notes, and review comments alongside the prose.

## 6. Let the explanation unfold {#present}

In **Slides**, compose a slide from the same plot sources. Add a beat for the next part of your explanation, then use the animation tools to reveal an element or transform it into a later state. Present at your own pace.

An interactive slide can also live inside a Paper document. HTML preserves its steps; PDF and Word use a still. The example below runs in Flux’s native player: the slides were composed for this website, and the plots come unchanged from the master demonstration project.

```{=html}
<div class="slide-demo" id="slide-demo" data-demo-src="/demos/data-morph/index.html" data-demo-scene="1">
<button type="button" class="demo-launch" aria-label="Load the interactive population slides" data-demo-start><img src="/assets/media/slide-poster.svg" alt="A response atlas of 143 visual neurons. Load the native slides to explore the study." width="1200" height="760" loading="lazy"><span class="demo-launch-prompt"><span class="play-disc" aria-hidden="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path d="m9 6 9 6-9 6Z" /></svg></span><span>Play the slides<small>Real Flux slides, running in your browser</small></span></span></button>
</div>
```

The example opens on **Follow the same cells**: 143 recorded cells in a shared response space, morphing between three stimulus frequencies. Use the arrows to advance, or choose another slide from the deck menu. Data: [Allen Institute for Brain Science](https://brain-map.org/our-research/circuits-behavior/visual-coding); the movement between states is illustrative interpolation. [Visual credits](/docs/visual-credits.html) · [Slides guide](/docs/slides.html).

## 7. Export and keep the sources {#export}

In Paper, choose **Export** and select PDF. Flux’s built-in PDF export does not require Quarto. Word export uses Quarto; install it through **Set up Flux** if needed. The command-line route, `flux compile --to pdf`, uses Quarto and also needs TeX ([PDF dependencies](/docs/export-documents.html#pdf-dependencies)).

Check the exported figures, captions, and references, then keep your project folder alongside the result. It contains the editable work you will want for the next revision.
